stem: A young child has fever, drooling, dysphagia, respiratory distress, and sits leaning forward in a tripod position. Which condition is most concerning?

options.B: An uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection.
options.C: A benign skin eruption without airway involvement.

rationale: Pediatric epiglottitis is a life-threatening upper-airway disorder. Classic findings include fever, drooling, dysphagia, respiratory distress/air hunger, and tripod positioning. Suspected pediatric epiglottitis requires urgent airway-focused management and unnecessary throat manipulation should be avoided. Therefore A is correct.
educational_objective: Recognize the pediatric epiglottitis pattern as a threatened-airway emergency.
source_locator: History and Physical — pediatric 3 Ds and tripod position; Evaluation/Treatment — avoid airway-provoking examination and prioritize airway management
source_claim_supported: Children with epiglottitis may have fever, drooling, dysphagia, respiratory distress and tripod positioning; airway compromise can progress rapidly and throat manipulation can precipitate deterioration.
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation — acute upper-airway obstruction and pediatric emergency recognition
correction_summary: Removed the over-specific claim that cough must be absent and focused on the strongly supported drooling/dysphagia/distress/tripod pattern and threatened airway. Reduced difficulty from hard to easy.
audit_findings: Current NCBI chapter directly supports A and cautions against unnecessary pediatric throat manipulation. The final item does not depend on an absolute absence of cough. Independent second pass passed.
